stories.headline: Denver, Latino groups sue to block ICE agents from polling places ahead of November election
stories.summary:
The city of Denver, the League of United Latin American Citizens and other voting rights groups filed a federal lawsuit Thursday seeking to prevent armed Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers from conducting enforcement operations at polling places during November's election. The suit, filed in federal court in Washington, D.C., argues that a Department of Homeland Security policy confirmed Sept. 1 by Secretary Markwayne Mullin authorizes ICE agents to serve warrants and detain people at polling locations, in violation of a law barring armed federal authorities from such sites since the Civil War.

Denver Mayor Mike Johnston and City Clerk and Recorder Paul Lopez both voiced support for the legal action. Johnston said the presence of armed agents near polling places is intended to intimidate voters and suppress turnout, calling the right to vote without fear 'fundamental to our democracy.'

A DHS spokesperson said the agency is not planning targeted operations at polling locations but left open the possibility of arrests if officials determine there is 'an active public safety threat.' The lawsuit cites ICE enforcement actions at polling sites in San Antonio, Ventura County and Syracuse earlier this year, though no such incidents have been documented in Colorado.

Colorado conducts most of its voting by mail, but Denver officials expressed concern that armed agents could appear at voting centers, drop boxes or early voting sites, potentially deterring residents from returning ballots and disrupting election operations.

stories.headline: Denver Mayor Johnston proposes $1.68 billion budget for 2027, projects modest revenue growth
stories.summary:
Mayor Mike Johnston released his proposed 2027 general fund budget of $1.68 billion on Thursday, projecting about 1.1% overall revenue growth compared to the current year — a modest upturn after several years of fiscal constraints. Johnston attributed the improvement in part to increased visitor spending downtown, particularly along the renovated 16th Street Mall, where sales tax revenue jumped 18% in June compared to the same month last year.

Sales taxes, which account for more than half of Denver's annual revenue, are projected to grow by about 5% compared to 2025. However, those gains are partially offset by declining property tax collections and reduced state marijuana revenue share-backs.

The proposed budget would partly replenish the city's reserve fund, which had slipped to nearly 10% of expenditures — well below the recommended 15% target. The 2027 plan aims to bring reserves back to 12%. Proposed new spending would go toward parks, pedestrian infrastructure, homelessness services, affordable housing, behavioral health, and the Denver Sheriff and Fire departments.

The budget comes roughly a year after the city laid off 169 employees and eliminated hundreds of vacant positions due to stagnating revenues. City Council budget hearings begin the week of Sept. 21, with a required passage deadline of Nov. 9.

stories.headline: Colorado regulators move to impose stricter air pollution limits on Suncor refinery in Commerce City
stories.summary:
Colorado air quality regulators are drafting tougher emissions rules for the Suncor refinery in Commerce City, the state's only oil refinery and a repeat violator of pollution standards. The Air Pollution Control Division plans to bring the proposed rules before the Air Quality Control Commission in December, with a final vote expected in early 2027. The new limits would require Suncor to install new equipment and adopt procedures to reduce toxic gas emissions from the facility's visible flares.

The refinery, owned by the highly profitable Canadian tar sands producer Suncor Energy, has repeatedly run afoul of state regulators for accidents and restarts that emit benzene, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxide and other pollutants over heavily populated north Denver and south Adams County neighborhoods. Colorado issued a $10.5 million penalty against Suncor in February 2024 — the largest ever against a single facility — and three additional potential violations from 2024 and 2025 remain under investigation.

Air Pollution Control Division Director Michael Ogletree said a commissioned third-party study comparing Suncor's operations to other U.S. refineries revealed that peer facilities are employing practices and technologies that could further cut emissions. 'We have the information we need to really aggressively go after measures to help continue to improve emissions,' he said.

Suncor said it has made significant investments in environmental improvements since 2005 and will continue working with regulators, while cautioning that new rules could affect its ability to compete with out-of-state fuel suppliers. The refinery supplies most of Colorado's vehicle fuel and a significant share of jet fuel at Denver International Airport.

stories.headline: One year after Evergreen High School shooting, students and community reflect on healing
stories.summary:
Thursday marked one year since a shooting at Evergreen High School critically injured two students before the gunman killed himself. Investigators determined the shooter had been drawn into extremist material online in the months before the attack, though a definitive motive was never confirmed. The shooting shook the small mountain community about 28 miles southwest of Denver and drew law enforcement response from across the metro area.

The Jefferson County school district offered students, staff and families a range of optional activities this week to mark the anniversary, including a gathering at the Lake House. District officials emphasized that participation in all events is entirely voluntary and that families choosing to keep students home on the anniversary would have absences excused.

'There is no single right way to experience these days,' the district said in a statement, underscoring its approach of care, connection and respect for different grieving processes. The district has also continued piecing together the circumstances leading up to the attack, including the shooter's documented online activity.

Senior Echo Robbins described a community that has grown stronger while still carrying grief. 'I'm feeling a lot better. I think all of us have healed and grown up a lot since that day,' she told Denver7. 'We're all a lot stronger, and I think it's impactful.'

stories.headline: Colorado records hottest summer on record as global temperatures also hit all-time highs
stories.summary:
Colorado averaged 69.4 degrees Fahrenheit across meteorological summer — June, July and August — this year, the highest seasonal average temperature recorded in the state since records began in 1895, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data. The previous state record of 68.7 degrees was set in 2012. Nationally, the contiguous United States also posted its hottest summer and hottest August on record.

Globally, this summer tied 2024 as the hottest on record, and August alone was the world's single hottest month ever documented, with average global temperatures reaching 62.53 degrees, according to the European Union's Copernicus Climate Change Service.

The record heat aligns with and helps explain a range of drought-driven impacts across Colorado this summer, including early fall foliage, campground closures due to dry water wells, and elevated wildfire risk. Climate scientists and advocacy groups cited the data as evidence of accelerating climate change driven by greenhouse gas emissions.

'There's no more room for doubt — the deaths and devastation we've witnessed in the past few months are the imprints of a planet on fire,' said Anne Jellema, executive director of the global climate organization 350.org, in a statement responding to the report.

stories.headline: Colorado wildlife officials kill three wolves in three days amid livestock predation conflicts
stories.summary:
Colorado Parks and Wildlife killed three young wolves between Sept. 7 and Sept. 10, shooting yearlings from the Copper Creek, Three Rivers and One Ear packs after the animals repeatedly preyed on livestock across Pitkin, Rio Blanco and Grand counties. CPW said each decision was made in consultation with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and in accordance with federal rules classifying Colorado's wolves as a nonessential experimental population, which permits lethal removal when wolves attack livestock more than three times in a 30-day period. Ranchers affected had employed a range of nonlethal deterrents including camera monitoring, nightly range rider patrols, and hazing devices.

The three killings bring to six the total number of wolves CPW has lethally removed since May 2026. Conservation groups raised concerns about the pace of removals, noting that the reintroduction program began with 25 wolves imported from Oregon and British Columbia between December 2023 and January 2025, of which only 12 adults imported during that period remain alive. Five packs have formed and produced pups, but federal restrictions have blocked further wolf imports since January.

Wolf advocate Courtney Vail of the Rocky Mountain Wolf Project questioned the precision with which CPW identified the specific wolves responsible for livestock deaths, particularly since the animals were uncollared. She also noted that killing female yearlings carries a greater long-term cost to the population's reproductive capacity than removing males.

CPW spokesperson Luke Perkins said the agency carefully weighs which wolves to remove, taking breeding success and pup safety into account. The state's wolf management plan calls for a target population of 150 to 200 wolves, a figure that remains far off given current mortality rates.

stories.headline: BLM ignored elk and deer migration corridors in Colorado oil and gas lease sales, lawsuit claims
stories.summary:
Two environmental groups filed suit in federal district court in Denver on Tuesday, seeking to overturn Bureau of Land Management oil and gas lease sales held in June that covered roughly 430 square miles across Colorado and Wyoming. The Carbondale-based Wilderness Workshop and the national Wilderness Society argue that BLM failed to account for vital migration corridors used by elk, pronghorn and mule deer when conducting environmental assessments for the auctions.

The June 15 Colorado sale — the largest on record for the state — offered 170 parcels totaling more than 155,000 acres, primarily in Moffat and Rio Blanco counties. About 86% of the parcels were leased, generating nearly $35.3 million in receipts. The lawsuit contends that BLM's interpretation of the Trump administration's One Big Beautiful Bill Act conflicts with other federal statutes requiring wildlife migration routes to be considered.

Both the Colorado and Wyoming governors have issued executive orders designating wildlife migration corridors as a priority resource. Colorado's Rocky Mountain elk herd, numbering about 250,000, is the largest in the country, and some herds in northwest Colorado undertake migrations of up to 70 miles between seasonal ranges.

The Department of the Interior declined to comment on the pending litigation. BLM is on pace to offer more than 400,000 acres of Colorado public land in lease sales across six auctions spanning December 2025 through December 2026.

stories.headline: Colorado's Office of Information Technology rehires 15 of 173 laid-off workers, reports $6 million in savings
stories.summary:
More than three months after laying off 173 workers as part of a reorganization, the Governor's Office of Information Technology has rehired just 15 of those employees, according to legislative testimony given Tuesday. The agency had simultaneously announced 98 new positions at the time of the May 27 layoffs, leaving many former state technology workers still unemployed in a difficult job market.

New OIT Director Sarah Tuneberg, who took over June 1, told the legislature's Joint Technology Committee that the reorganization has already yielded at least $6 million in platform savings through vendor renegotiations, including a 10% reduction in Google Cloud costs. Additional savings came from using artificial intelligence at the Department of Corrections to reduce manual coding hours and from cutting what the agency described as administrative overhead at the Colorado Department of Public Safety.

OIT has faced sustained criticism over the past year for failing to implement cybersecurity recommendations from the State Auditor's Office and for low customer satisfaction scores from other state agencies it serves. Tuneberg cited improvements including reducing the time low-income families spend accessing a children's food benefit to 25 seconds from two minutes, and noted that the state's myColorado digital driver's license is now accepted at airport security by the TSA.

Former OIT employees told the Colorado Sun many are still struggling to find work and feel the abrupt nature of the layoffs was poorly handled after years of public service. The agency said further savings are expected as it continues consolidating software tools and renegotiating vendor contracts.

stories.headline: Parker driver arrested on vehicular homicide charge after crash that killed 18-year-old passenger
stories.summary:
An 18-year-old Parker man was arrested on suspicion of vehicular homicide after a two-car crash Tuesday night that killed a passenger in his vehicle. The victim, identified by the Douglas County Coroner's Office as Talon Gustafson, was ejected from the car near the intersection of Mainstreet and Motsenbocker Road in Parker shortly after 11 p.m. He was transported to a hospital by South Metro Fire Rescue paramedics but did not survive.

The driver, Chase Murphy, 18, faces charges of vehicular homicide by reckless driving, reckless driving and speeding 40 mph or more over the posted speed limit. The speed limit in the area is 40 mph, meaning Murphy is accused of traveling at least 80 mph at the time of the crash. No injuries were reported to occupants of the second vehicle involved in the collision.

Parker police said speed is believed to have been the primary factor in the crash. A department traffic enforcement map showed more than a dozen traffic stops in the area between 2025 and 2026, though the intersection had not been flagged as a frequent complaint location, with only one speeding concern reported there this year.

The Parker Police Department made more than 8,800 traffic stops in 2025 and has logged over 5,500 so far in 2026. Residents can flag unsafe driving locations through an online portal, police said.

stories.headline: Former Wheat Ridge motel site sells for $16.5 million; 335-unit apartment complex planned
stories.summary:
The former American Motel property along Interstate 70 in Wheat Ridge sold last week for $16.5 million to Dallas-based Trinsic Residential Group, which plans to build 335 apartments on the 5.8-acre site. The buyer and seller finalized the deal after years of delays involving a zoning code conflict, asbestos remediation complications, utility capacity disputes with Xcel Energy, and a dispute with the Colorado Department of Transportation over an alleged construction moratorium that CDOT later acknowledged was in error.

Seller Tony Sherman, an Aspen-based hospitality investor, purchased the property in January 2023 for $9 million, originally considering converting the half-century-old motel into a Marriott-branded hotel before pivoting to a land sale strategy after concluding the property was worth more without the structure. The city of Wheat Ridge supported the project throughout, and its urban renewal authority earmarked $9 million toward demolition and future development costs.

The American Motel was a longtime landmark in the Denver suburb, known for its large red sign advertising rooms at $32.95 per night and notable for having hosted Elvis Presley during a 1976 visit. Sherman ultimately demolished the building at the buyer's insistence as delays mounted and market conditions softened.

Sherman said the lengthy process cost him significant time and leverage as interest rates rose and the apartment market weakened. Despite the complications, he described the underlying bet — that the raw land was more valuable than the operating motel — as sound from the start.

stories.headline: Michelin Guide set to expand Colorado restaurant ratings statewide for first time on Sept. 14
stories.summary:
The Michelin Guide will announce its 2026 Colorado restaurant selections on Monday, Sept. 14, marking the fourth year the guide has operated in the state and the first time it will venture beyond the six original territories of Denver, Boulder, Aspen, Vail, Snowmass Village and Beaver Creek Resort. New coverage will include Aurora, Fort Collins, Grand Junction, Breckenridge, Telluride, Colorado Springs, Crested Butte and other communities.

The current Colorado guide lists 49 restaurants, nine of which hold stars and 10 of which carry Bib Gourmand designations for quality at a moderate price. Critics and observers expect those numbers to at least double with the expanded geographic scope, and some are watching to see whether contenders outside the traditional resort corridors — such as Rootstalk in Breckenridge or Bin 707 Foodbar in Grand Junction — will be considered for star recognition.

The guide has drawn criticism over the years for awarding stars almost exclusively to chef's counter-style restaurants offering a single tasting menu per night. Seven of the nine current starred restaurants in Colorado fit that format, and food writers are watching to see whether the 2026 guide broadens its recognition to dining in more varied settings.

The guide's expansion is significant for Colorado's broader restaurant industry, as Michelin recognition routinely drives tourism and reservations. All six original territories contributed financially to a state fund that brought the guide to Colorado in 2023; communities added in the 2026 expansion will now benefit from that investment.

stories.headline: Denver photographer who gave world first images of Ground Zero reflects on 9/11 anniversary
stories.summary:
Michael Rieger, a Denver-based FEMA photographer, provided the world with some of its earliest images of Ground Zero following the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks, spending weeks working on the debris field known as 'the pile' in lower Manhattan. CPR News profiled Rieger on the 25th anniversary of the attacks, examining the lasting impact of his documentation work and his experience as one of the first photojournalists to capture the scale of the destruction.

Rieger's images, taken in an official capacity for the federal emergency management agency, became part of the historical record of the worst terrorist attack on American soil. His work illustrates the role Colorado-based federal and emergency personnel played in the national response to the attacks.

topStory.headline: Nation Marks 25th Anniversary of Sept. 11 Attacks With Ceremonies in New York, Virginia and Pennsylvania
topStory.summary:
The United States on Friday observed the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, which killed 2,977 people at the World Trade Center in New York, the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and in a field near Shanksville, Pennsylvania. Remembrance ceremonies were held at all three sites, drawing victims' families, first responders, elected officials and former heads of state.

President Donald Trump attended the Pentagon ceremony, marking his second consecutive year observing the anniversary at that site after attending the Ground Zero ceremony in 2024. Vice President JD Vance represented the administration in New York, joining four former presidents — Joe Biden, Barack Obama, George W. Bush and Bill Clinton — as well as former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton at the Ground Zero ceremony. Other administration officials traveled to Shanksville for that site's observance.

At the National September 11 Memorial and Museum in lower Manhattan, organizers introduced a seventh moment of silence this year, added to the traditional six that mark the sequence of attacks. The new moment honors those who have died from illnesses and injuries connected to the attacks — a toll that now exceeds 9,000 and surpasses the number killed on the day itself. Museum CEO Beth Hillman noted that the 25-year milestone is a reminder that many Americans have no personal memory of the attacks, underscoring the importance of continued commemoration.

Personal accounts of the day continued to surface as the anniversary approached. Robert Schnelle, the first NYPD K-9 officer on the scene, recalled sheltering with his rescue dog Atlas as the South Tower collapsed, then working 12-hour shifts at Ground Zero for eight months. Firefighter Stephen Siller, who died in the attacks after running through the Brooklyn Battery Tunnel in full gear to reach the towers, was honored through a procession Friday retracing his final route, organized by the Tunnel to Towers Foundation. Earlier in the week, a 21-foot steel beam recovered from the South Tower was displayed at the Ellipse near the White House as part of a national tour. Trump on Wednesday issued a proclamation designating Friday as Patriot Day 2026.
